figure: Figure A.1 — Extreme sparsity: four selected families (2026)
issue: The chart places four bars on a single 'Active fraction' axis even though the Qwen bar uses a different denominator (125B backbone only, excluding 51B n-gram and 4B MTP) and the caption says the four bars are 'not one like-for-like series'. The asterisk and footnote are present, but the visual encoding still invites direct comparison of bar lengths. The caveat is carried mainly by small gray annotation text.
evidence: Qwen row: '*4.8%' with annotation '125B backbone/6B active (+51B n-gram, 4B MTP)'. Footnote: '* Qwen bar = backbone ratio (125B backbone), excluding the 51B n-gram embedding and 4B MTP.' Caption: 'denominators differ by vendor and the Qwen bar is its 125 B backbone only, so the four bars are not one like-for-like series'.
acceptance_test: Either visually separate the Qwen bar (e.g., a distinct panel or a clear break/annotation) or add an explicit in-figure warning at readable size that bar lengths are not directly comparable across rows. A reader should not have to read the footnote to avoid treating the four bars as a single ranked series.

figure: Figure A.2 — Vendor-reported ratios: % remaining
issue: The scope annotations that carry the figure's central caveat are set in small, low-contrast gray type, while the bold percentages dominate. A reader scanning the table can easily take '~7%', '~10%', '~23%', and '~33%' as comparable cross-model numbers and miss that the DeepSeek rows are single-token whole-model ratios while the GLM rows are per-layer/per-head ratios.
evidence: The table's main numbers are large and bold; the qualifying text ('single-token KV cache', 'single-token inference FLOPs', 'per-layer KV (BF16)', 'attention only per head / layer') is small gray text beneath each row. The red warning box says 'no shared scale', but the scope text that explains why is visually subordinate.
acceptance_test: At print size, the scope text for each row is at least as legible as the footnote and is visually attached to the number it qualifies; a reader can state the scope of each row without reading the caption.

figure: Figure A.3 — A chronology of frontier AI systems
issue: The figure is drawn as a stack of touching horizontal bars, which visually encodes cumulative layering or substrate dependency. The caption explicitly says it is 'not a substrate stack' and 'not a causal lineage', but the visual form contradicts the caption. A reader can reasonably infer that each stage builds on or requires the previous one, which is the opposite of the intended claim.
evidence: The bars are stacked vertically with no gaps, each sitting directly on the one below, and the caption has to negate the visual: 'not a causal lineage and not a substrate stack: a later stage does not require the one before it'. The dates are listed to the right, not positioned on a time axis, so the stack is the dominant visual encoding.
acceptance_test: The figure no longer reads as a stack or dependency chain without the caption; a reader shown only the figure can correctly say that the stages are a chronology of selected milestones, not a cumulative stack.

figure: Figure A.4 — Where Should Intelligence Live?
issue: The band 'Inside post-training (build-time)' is colored blue, which the legend defines as 'system-side', but post-training is a model-building process that shapes the weights and is conceptually model-side. It also has no chapter reference, unlike every other band. The result is a taxonomic inconsistency: the figure places a build-time model process in the system-side group and leaves it unmapped to the book's chapters.
evidence: Legend: 'blue = system-side · green = model-side'. The band 'Inside post-training (build-time)' is blue and sits above the green model-side bands. Every other band has a chapter reference (Ch18, Ch20; Ch17–20, Ch24; Ch19, Ch24; Ch22; Ch10; Ch7, Ch8; Ch3, Ch8); this band has none.
acceptance_test: The post-training band is either recolored/moved to the model-side group with an appropriate chapter reference, or the caption explicitly explains why build-time post-training is classified as system-side and why it has no chapter mapping.

figure: Figure A.5 — Shared weights do not remove executed work
issue: The legend says 'Dashed arrows = weight reuse', but dashed arrows are also used from each pass down to its iteration history cache. Those arrows represent cache/history state, not weight reuse. The same line style therefore carries two different meanings, and the legend does not define the cache-state meaning.
evidence: Top section: dashed arrows run from 'one shared core weight set' to pass 1/pass 2/pass 3 (weight reuse), and dashed arrows also run from each pass down to 'iteration 1 history cache', 'iteration 2 history cache', and 'iteration 3 history cache'. The legend at the bottom defines only 'Dashed arrows = weight reuse'.
acceptance_test: Weight reuse and history-cache state use visually distinct line styles, and the legend defines both; a reader can tell which dashed arrows mean weight reuse and which mean cache state.

figure: Figure A.5 — Shared weights do not remove executed work
issue: In the 'Actual stop' row, the path is drawn as pass 1 → pass 2 → pass 3 (not executed) → exit. This visually puts the non-executed pass on the runtime path, contradicting the caption's claim that 'a true exit omits later work'. The reader cannot tell whether pass 3 is bypassed or merely marked as not executed while still being traversed.
evidence: The 'Actual stop' row shows a solid arrow from pass 2 into the dashed box 'pass 3 (not executed)', then an arrow from that box to 'exit'. The caption says 'A true exit omits later work'; the legend says 'dashed box = not executed'. If pass 3 is not executed, the exit should branch from pass 2 directly, not pass through the non-executed box.
acceptance_test: The 'Actual stop' path shows pass 2 → exit directly, with pass 3 ghosted off the path or omitted; a reader can immediately see that pass 3 is skipped rather than traversed.

figure: Figure A.5 — Shared weights do not remove executed work
issue: The dashed box 'pass 3 (not executed)' and its connecting arrows are low-contrast light gray. At print size, the dashed outline and the text inside are harder to read than the solid boxes, which weakens the figure's ability to communicate the skipped-work distinction.
evidence: The 'pass 3 (not executed)' box is drawn in light gray with a dashed border, while the executed passes are dark-bordered boxes with black text. The dashed arrows around it are also light.
acceptance_test: The non-executed pass remains visually distinct but its label and outline are legible at print size and in grayscale without squinting.

figure: Figure 7.5
issue: The inline annotations ('9.5K max context ...', '8× savings ...', '~436 GB budget at 166K') are set noticeably smaller than the axis/legend text and are difficult to read at print size; the dense annotation text also competes with the plotted lines.
evidence: At 150 dpi the annotation glyphs are visibly smaller than the axis tick labels and legend; the '8× savings...' line is a long string placed inside the plot area.
acceptance_test: All figure annotations measure at least 8 pt at print size, or the detail is moved into the caption/legend with only short leader labels left in the plot.

figure: Figure 7.3
issue: The figure states 'No compatible kernel: reject; fallback is not guaranteed.' The caption says 'Unsupported combinations may be rejected; fallback is not guaranteed.' The figure's unqualified 'reject' is stronger than the caption and can be read as a universal guarantee of rejection, whereas some runtimes may fall back to a slower path or fail differently.
evidence: Figure text: 'No compatible kernel: reject; fallback is not guaranteed.' Caption: 'Unsupported combinations may be rejected; fallback is not guaranteed.'
acceptance_test: Figure text matches the caption's modality, e.g. 'No compatible kernel: may reject; fallback is not guaranteed' or 'cannot execute without a compatible kernel'.

figure: Figure 7.3
issue: The arrows from 'Error-control method' and 'Numerical representation' terminate on the outer 'Container wraps tensors + metadata' box rather than on the 'Packed tensor' box. This blurs the distinction the caption draws between the packed tensor and the checkpoint container.
evidence: In Figure 7.3 the two top boxes' downward arrows enter the top edge of the large container box; the 'Packed tensor: values + scales...' box sits inside that container and receives no arrow.
acceptance_test: Arrows terminate on the packed-tensor box, or the container is clearly drawn as a downstream wrapper after packing.

figure: Figure 6.2
issue: The 'sample p99' label is placed at the top left of the plot, far from the red dashed 1.33 s line it names, and has no leader. A reader can momentarily associate the label with the nearby p50/p90/p95 cluster instead of the 1.33 s line.
evidence: In Figure 6.2 the red 'sample p99' text sits above the green p50 label near x≈0.8, while the red dashed sample-p99 line is at x≈1.33; the boxed note 'sample p99 (interpolation) = 1.33s' is the only direct tie.
acceptance_test: The 'sample p99' label is adjacent to the 1.33 s line or connected by a leader; no ambiguity remains at print size.

figure: Figure 7.6
issue: The bar fills use hatching on the inference and QLoRA bars but a solid fill on the full fine-tune bar, with no legend or caption explaining what the pattern encodes. This is a gratuitous visual distinction that can imply a semantic difference where none is stated.
evidence: Figure 7.6: inference bar is blue with diagonal hatching; QLoRA bar is green with diagonal hatching; full fine-tune bar is solid red. The caption and in-figure notes describe only the quantities, not the fill patterns.
acceptance_test: Either the hatching encodes a stated distinction (and is explained in the caption/legend), or all bars use a consistent fill treatment.

figure: Figure 7.7 — Concurrency budget — one 8×H100 host
issue: The faint vertical rules said to mark 24.9 GB request slots inside the KV band are not visually distinguishable from the orange dotted fill. The figure therefore does not actually communicate the 17-request slot decomposition it claims to show; the reader must rely on the equation below.
evidence: Caption: “the faint vertical rules inside the KV band mark those 24.9 GB request slots.” In the rendered figure, the KV band is filled with a regular white-dot pattern; no separate slot-boundary rules are legible at print size. The equation below the bar carries the entire 436 ÷ 24.9 ≈ 17.5 → ~17 message.
acceptance_test: At 100% print size, a reader can distinguish 17 slot boundaries from the decorative fill pattern without reading the caption or equation. If the slot boundaries are not intended to be countable, remove the claim that they mark request slots and let the equation carry the arithmetic.

figure: Figure 7.8 — Memory Tetris
issue: The 80 GB rank-boundary lines are unlabeled and visually merge with the ordinary horizontal grid. The caption says they are a visualization guide, but the figure itself gives no key distinguishing rank boundaries from grid lines, so the reader cannot tell which lines carry the per-rank caveat.
evidence: Caption: “(light rules = 80 GB rank boundaries)” and “the 80 GB rank-boundary lines are a visualization guide.” The chart shows several light horizontal rules, but no line is marked or keyed as a rank boundary; the 640 GB dashed line is the only annotated horizontal reference.
acceptance_test: A reader can identify which horizontal rules are the 80 GB rank boundaries without reading the caption, e.g. by a distinct line style, a single labeled example, or a small legend entry.

figure: Figure 8.1 — Where inference computation and data movement actually live
issue: The compute box “tensor cores / ALU” is placed inside the vertical memory-hierarchy ladder, and the red gradient arrow “capacity grows / speed drops / distance grows” spans the entire stack including that compute box. This visually implies that tensor cores/ALU are a level of the memory hierarchy, contradicting the caption’s statement that compute, memory, and interconnect are separate groups.
evidence: Caption: “the figure groups the resources three ways: compute units (tensor cores/ALU); the memory hierarchy … and interconnect” and “only the memory hierarchy is a smallest-to-largest ladder.” In the figure, the blue compute box sits between registers and shared memory, and the red gradient arrow runs past it as if it were a rung on the same ladder.
acceptance_test: A reader can tell at a glance that tensor cores/ALU are a separate compute group, not a memory level, and that the speed/capacity/distance gradient applies only to the memory hierarchy. This may require offsetting the compute box, breaking the gradient arrow around it, or adding a visual bracket that separates compute from the memory ladder.

figure: Figure 8.1 — Where inference computation and data movement actually live
issue: White labels over dense orange and green crosshatch fills have reduced contrast, especially the smaller secondary lines such as “fastest · smallest,” “on-chip · close,” “on-die,” and “large · slower.” The pattern competes with the text at print size.
evidence: The figure uses a high-frequency crosshatch behind white text in the registers, shared-memory, L2, HBM, GPU-interconnect, and remote-GPU boxes. The primary labels remain readable, but the secondary lines are visibly busier than the same text would be on a solid fill.
acceptance_test: At 100% print size, every label and secondary annotation remains comfortably readable without zooming, and the fill pattern does not create shimmer or legibility loss in grayscale.

figure: Figure 8.2 — Per-GPU roofline: dense FP16, one H100 vs one H200
issue: The annotation “decode batch B=8 (intensity ≈ B FLOP/byte)” uses a long arrow that crosses the H100 roofline and points to a small marker. The reading order is not immediate: the eye must trace a long connector across the plot to associate the label with the correct point.
evidence: The label sits in the left-middle region of the chart, while the B=8 point is near x ≈ 8 on the H100 line. The arrow crosses the blue H100 line and passes near other annotations, making the association less direct than the other point labels.
acceptance_test: A reader can associate the B=8 label with its point within a few seconds without tracing a connector across unrelated lines, e.g. by placing the label closer to the point or using a short leader line.

figure: Figure 8.3 — Wan2.2 TI2V-5B whole-clip denoising
issue: The feedback loop on the right side of the Wan2.2 box is drawn with the same solid line style that the legend defines as “data/state flow,” but the loop represents denoising/scheduler iteration — a control/iteration loop, not a data/state flow. The figure therefore does not visually distinguish control flow from data flow, even though the caption explicitly says the loop is “denoising/scheduler iteration, not architectural recurrence.”
evidence: Legend: “Solid: data/state flow. Dashed: denoiser conditioning.” The loop arrow from the right side of the Wan2.2 box back into the same box is solid. Caption: “The feedback loop is denoising/scheduler iteration, not architectural recurrence.”
acceptance_test: A reader can tell from the figure alone, without the caption, that the loop is a control/iteration loop rather than a data/state dependency. This requires a distinct line style, a loop-specific label, or an explicit control-flow legend entry.

figure: Figure 9.1 — Ring traffic and directional bandwidth
issue: The annotation says “140 GB tensor” while the x-axis and surrounding prose define the quantity as logical input tensor per rank. A reader can misread the annotation as a 140 GB total tensor rather than 140 GB per rank.
evidence: The x-axis label is “Logical input tensor per rank (GB)”; the annotation reads “140 GB tensor (245 GB sent at 1.75×)”; the caption says “At 140 GB the ideal times are about 0.54 s, 6.1 s and 98 s.” The prose on printed p. 162 says the eight-rank ring “sends 245 GB per rank.”
acceptance_test: Change the annotation to “140 GB per rank” or “140 GB logical tensor per rank,” and verify the caption uses the same per-rank qualifier at least once.

figure: Figure 9.2 — SUM first; replication second
issue: The parenthetical “(8 B/rank)” is ambiguous: it can be read as the amount each rank sends, but the figure later states each rank sends 12 B across both phases. The 8 B is the input size per rank, not the communication volume.
evidence: The figure header says “Four ranks; four FP16 elements per input (8 B/rank).” The reduce-scatter and all-gather annotations each say “6 B sent + 6 B received/rank,” and the bottom box says “Per rank: 12 B sent + 12 B received = 24 B endpoint total.”
acceptance_test: Replace “(8 B/rank)” with “(8 B input per rank)” or “(8 B payload per rank before communication),” and confirm the caption still states the 12 B sent / 12 B received total.
